extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, art critics, students of architecture and aesthetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Critical standards for judging and producing architecture and art (with a focus on Renaissance practice): balance between knowledge and wonder; human sympathy and ornament; scale versus detail; uses of scholarship; moral/spiritual aims of design. Emphasises aesthetic and ethical criteria rather than technical prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure in knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: It is for each man to find his own measure in this matter; in great part, also, for others to find it for him, while he is yet a youth. The desperate evil of the whole Renaissance system is, that all idea of measure is therein forgotten, that knowledge is thought the one and only good, and it is never inquired whether men are vivified by it or paralyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek a personal, balanced amount of learning appropriate to the individual and vocation. Avoid treating knowledge as an absolute good without testing whether it animates the person or stifles life; teachers and institutions should help discover this measure for youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve wonder and continual discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The real animating power of knowledge is only in the moment of its being first received...a joy for which the previous ignorance is just as necessary as the present knowledge. That man is always happy who is in the presence of something which he cannot know to the full, which he is always going on to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and education should cultivate ongoing curiosity: artistic practice values the continual discovery of ‘new ignorance’ and the delight of learning, rather than the settled triumph of fully familiarized knowledge. Anti-pattern: treating mastery as an end that kills wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid knowledge that deadens imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: One effect of knowledge is to deaden the force of the imagination and the original energy of the whole man: under the weight of his knowledge he cannot move so lightly as in the days of his simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forms of study and technical training that integrate with imaginative freedom (knowledge like chain-mail that folds with the body), and avoid ‘armor of plate’—forms of scholarship that bind, cramp or gall the artist. Evaluate teaching by whether it preserves agility and creative impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge must be personally earned and fashioned
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no part of the furniture of a man's mind which he has a right to exult in, but that which he has hewn and fashioned for himself...if he has done none of these things, but only had it thrown in his face by a passer-by, what cause has he to be proud? Knowledge is like current coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value original thought and skills that are discovered or crafted by the practitioner. Anti-pattern: pride in received, unassimilated scholarship; institutions should encourage personal work, not mere accumulation of others' learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception over mere classification and catalogue-making
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the science, but the perception, to which the good is owing; and the natural sciences may become as harmful as any others, when they lose themselves in classification and catalogue-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give precedence to perceptive seeing and understanding of nature rather than to mere taxonomies or exhaustive catalogs. Technical knowledge is valuable when it enlarges humility and perception; it is harmful when it becomes an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pride of scholarship and formalism over truth
rubrics_metrics.description: They discovered suddenly that the world for ten centuries had been living in an ungrammatical manner, and they made it forthwith the end of human existence to be grammatical. Falsehood in a Ciceronian dialect had no opposers; truth in patois no listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let mastery of forms (grammar, syntax, learned dialects, classical manner) substitute for truth, feeling, or accessible expression. Anti-patterns: valuing style or learned correctness above honesty of thought or popular intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture must show sympathy with common people
rubrics_metrics.description: All other architectures have something in them that common men can enjoy; some concession to the simplicities of humanity, some daily bread for the hunger of the multitude...Qua nt fancy, rich ornament, bright color, something that shows a sympathy with men of ordinary minds and hearts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should include elements that common people can enjoy (ornament, color, familiar forms). Evaluate buildings by whether they welcome and delight ordinary minds, not only the learned elite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid architecture as aristocratic exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Renaissance is rigid, cold, inhuman; incapable of glowing, of stooping, of conceding for an instant...I do not work for the vulgar, only for the men of the academy and the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist creating work that proclaims 'you cannot feel my work unless you study Vitruvius.' Aim for accessibility and warmth instead of deliberate exclusion or cold perfection. Examples of anti-patterns: inserting pedestals/columns in portraits to exalt status; turning a Nativity into a Corinthian arcade to show skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let architecture serve luxury and sensual indulgence over spiritual ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The dead Renaissance drew back into its earthliness...But it understood the luxury of the body; the terraced and scented and grottoed garden, with its trickling fountains and slumbrous shades...the frescoed wall and roof, covered with the last lasciviousness of Paganism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance domestic comfort with spiritual and moral purposes—avoid prioritizing bodily luxury, sensual decoration, or pagan lasciviousness at the expense of art's higher aims. Anti-pattern: buildings and decoration designed primarily to indulge elite bodily pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prefer colossal scale over craftsmanship and local detail
rubrics_metrics.description: They appealed for such approbation as they needed from the multitude, to the lowest possible standard of taste; and while the older workman lavished his labor on the minute niche and narrow casement...the Renaissance builder spared such cost and toil in his detail, that he might spend it in bringing larger stones from a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value careful, intimate workmanship and meaningful detail rather than using sheer magnitude to impress. Anti-patterns: sacrificing ornament and careful carving to achieve ‘colossal’ or ‘finished’ magnitude that only signals power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funerary art should express peaceful humility, not pride or terror
rubrics_metrics.description: The early tombs at once simple and lovely in adornment, severe and solemn in their expression; confessing the power, and accepting the peace, of death...the tombs of the later ages are a ghastly struggle of mean pride and miserable terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sepulchral design, prefer symbols of resignation, hope, and dignity (simple adornment, solemn expression) instead of elaborate self-exaltation or grotesque anxiety (over-polished portrait statues, scythed skeletons). Evaluate tombs by whether they comfort rather than flaunt or terrify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different branches of knowledge vary in tendency to feed pride
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly in proportion as they are inferior, nugatory, or limited in scope, their power of feeding pride is greater. Thus philology, logic, rhetoric, and the other sciences of the schools...have so pestilent an effect upon those who are devoted to them...but the true and great sciences...make men gentle and modest in proportion to the largeness of their apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or teaching disciplines, recognize that disciplines devoted to words and formal methods are more likely to foster pride and self-satisfaction; encourage study that enlarges humility and a sense of the infinite. Anti-pattern: elevating trivial learned skills as ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists must be rooted in enduring moral/spiritual traditions, not barren technical sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Those great Fathers were only able to receive such nourishment because they were rooted on the rock of all ages, and that our scientific teaching, nowadays, is nothing more nor less than the assiduous watering of trees whose stems are cut through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate grounding in long moral/spiritual traditions that nourish art; beware relying solely on contemporary scientific technique or 'barren' sciences to produce greatness. Examples: Raphael, Leonardo, Michelangelo had older religious/earnest roots; later followers lacked that root and produced barren dexterity. Anti-pattern: trying to manufacture genius by technical instruction alone.
